explanation:
The TOEFL iBT Listening section

The TOEFL iBT Listening section includes:

‣ Audios: 2 conversations and 3 lectures
‣ Length: About 3 minutes for each conversation and 3-5 minutes for each lecture.
‣ Questions: 5 questions for each conversation and 6 questions for each lecture.
‣ Time: About 36 minutes to complete this section

Important details

  • The audios are campus conversations and academic lectures, so both use language you would hear in a university setting.
  • You will listen to each conversation and lecture only once before you can see the questions.
  • You can take notes while you listen to help you answer the questions later.

Reading scores

Each of the four sections of the TOEFL iBT –Reading, Listening, Speaking, and Writing– is scored on a scale of 0-30, totaling 120 points. The proficiency levels for listening are:


‣ Advanced: 22-30

‣ High-Intermediate: 17-21

‣ Low-Intermediate: 9-16

‣ Below Low-Intermediate: 0-8

Scores provide personalized feedback and performance insights. Test takers receive instant scoring for the reading and listening sections, which means they can see their results immediately after completing these parts of the exam. There are no passing or failing scores; institutions set their own requirements. For more details, visit the TOEFL score understanding page.

Question types

Each conversation or lecture has a variety of questions, which may include:

  1. Gist-Content (Main Idea)
  2. Gist-Purpose – Primary Purpose
  3. Detail
  4. Function
  5. Attitude
  6. Organisation (lecture structure)
  7. Connecting content
  8. Inference

1. Gist-Content

Gist-content questions ask about the main topic or idea of the conversation or lecture. When the question appears, you will have four options; click the one that best sums up the main idea. Occasionally, where there are two main ideas in a lecture or conversation, you may be asked to choose two out of four options.

Gist-content or gist-purpose questions always come first, and there will be either a gist-content question or a gist-purpose question, but not both.

Gist-content questions usually have this sort of phrasing:

  • What is … mainly about?
  • What is/are … mainly discussing?
  • What’s the main topic of the lecture/discussion?
  • What is/are the main idea/s of the lecture?

2. Gist-Purpose

Gist-Purpose questions ask about why the conversation is taking place or why the lecturer is giving a talk.  You will be shown a question with four options; click the one that best sums up the primary purpose. Occasionally, where there are two main purposes for a conversation or lecture, so you may be asked to choose two out of four options.

Note that sometimes the main idea and the purpose can overlap.

Gist-purpose questions usually have this sort of phrasing:

  • Why does the student visit … ?
  • Why does the professor…?

3. Detail

Detail questions are about specific facts or ideas in the listening. They are often what questions. The idea will always be explicitly stated and will be about something important, so a minor detail will NOT be a correct answer.

Some examples of detail questions could be:

  • What does the professor/lecturer say about…?
  • According to the speaker, what is the key to…?
  • According to the lecture, what is an example of…?
  • Which of the following is an example/indicator of…?
  • According to… how…?

4. Function

Function questions focus on understanding the purpose behind a speaker’s statement. They ask you about the real meaning behind a phrase or sentence, why a speaker says something or what they imply by their statement. They are not asking for directly or literally stated information but rather require you to infer the speaker’s intention.

Typical phrasing for this type of question is:

  • What does the professor/student mean when he says…?
  • Why does the professor/student say…?

5. Attitude

Attitude questions are designed to determine the speaker’s attitude or their feelings, opinions, or perspective on a particular topic. These questions may require you to understand the tone, mood, or emotional state of the speaker based on how they express their ideas.

You will identify this type of questions because they include phrases like:

  • What is the speaker’s attitude towards…?
  • What attitude does the professor/student express when he/she says…?
  • What does the professor/student think about…?
  • How does … feel about…?

6. Organisation

Organisation questions only ask about lectures, and they test your ability to understand how a lecture is structured. They frequently focus on examples and ask why something is mentioned or discussed.

Organization questions often include phrases such as:

  • Why does the professor mention…?
  • Why does the professor discuss…?
  • The professor referst to … in order to…?

7. Connecting content

Connecting content questions look at the logical relationships between different parts of a conversation, or lecture.  You may have to identify steps in a process, identify cause and effect, put things into categories, or make a prediction based on what you’ve heard.

There are two question types:

  • Choose one or more correct answers in a multiple choice question
  • Drag choices into a table or chart

8. Inference

Inference questions are about what the conversation or lecture implies, or what we can guess from it.

questions.prompt: Why did Freya primarily go to see Professor Dubois?

choices.html: To discuss how to manage stress.
To seek advice about a presentation.
To clarify the deadline for an assignment.
To understand the scope of social media.

questions.prompt: What aspect of social media’s role in business is Freya most interested in?

choices.html: The speed at which it can effect change.
Its ability to target specific customers.
The fact that anyone can write posts.
Its relationship with certain age groups.

questions.prompt: Why does Freya mention TikTok during her conversation with Professor Dubois?

choices.html: To discuss its role in marketing and brand building.
To illustrate its influence on politics and public opinion.
To highlight the impact of social media on mental health.
To show the prevalence of fake news and misinformation.

questions.prompt: In Professor Dubois’s opinion, what is the most important aspect of Freya’s presentation?

choices.html: How much background knowledge Freya demonstrates .
How thorough the research behind it is.
How good the draft submitted on the 14th is.
How engaging the topic is for the audience.

questions.prompt: Why does the student say this in response to the professor?

choices.html: To disagree with what the professor has just said.
To agree with what the professor has just said.
To stress her lack of knowledge in the matter.
To complain about the number of assignments students have.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the lecture?

choices.html: Brand image reflects a company’s personality and values.
Brand image maintains customer loyalty through consistency.
Brand Image derives from an accumulation of customer feedback.
Brand image is everything customers think and feel about a brand.

questions.prompt: What does the professor mean when she says this?

choices.html: they must fully understand their target market.
they must try to control brand image as much as possible.
they must constantly get feedback from consumers.
they must resonate with their chosen demographic.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, what do companies risk when they deviate from their established brand values?

choices.html: Increasing their marketing costs.
Disaffecting their customers.
Reducing their product quality.
Losing market share to competitors.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker’s attitude towards Pepsi following the Kendall Jenner ad?

choices.html: He is shocked that the company ran the advertisement at all.
He believes the outcome would have been different at a different time.
He is surprised by the scale of the outrage the advert prompted.
He thinks Pepsi only have themselves to blame for any resulting losses.

questions.prompt:
The speaker says brand images evolve. Which brand does he mention as representative of change and which of consistency?
 
Change:                    Consistency:

What does the professor suggest when she says this?


Choose TWO answers.

choices.html: He has firsthand experience of brand building.
Ogilvy was a marketing company in the retail sector.
Brand Image matters critically for startup companies.
Brand image is chief determiner of success or failure.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason Sarah wants to move out of campus housing?

choices.html: She thinks the dormitories are unsafe.
She cannot afford the campus housing fees.
She finds the dorm environment distracting.
She wants to live closer to her friend at MIT.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about Sarah?

choices.html: She is a married student.
She is a final-year student.
She is a postgraduate student.
She is an international student.

questions.prompt:
Why does Sarah prefer not to make an official complaint about her current dorm situation?

Choose TWO answers

choices.html: She believes the issues are typical of dorm life.
She does not think she will be taken seriously.
She wants to avoid conflict and quietly move out.
She is afraid of retaliation from other students.

questions.prompt: What does Sarah need to do in order to terminate her housing contract?

choices.html: Pay a termination fee.
Submit a written request.
Discuss it with campus security.
Wait for the end of the semester.

questions.prompt: What does the housing officer mean when he says this?

choices.html: She will check on Sarah’s well-being after she moves off-campus.
She will need to be informed of Sarah’s movements for a while.
She will have to write a series of reports on Sarah for the university.
She will have to keep Sarah under surveillance until she has settled in.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the lecture?

choices.html: To consider the evolution and complexity of the English language
To detail the role of Norman French in the development of Old English.
To identify the events leading to the rise of an English-speaking aristocracy.
To discuss the influence of trade and colonial expansion on the English language.

questions.prompt: What does the existence of words like “cow” and “beef” illustrate?

choices.html: How Old English replaced Norman French.
How words from different languages started to coexist
How French words were not only used in legal matters.
How English words became dominant in Europe.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker mention the Norman Conquest? (Choose two options)

choices.html: To describe the linguistic differences it created between social classes.
To use as an example of French dominance.
To imply that English was a weaker language than French.
To highlight the influence that French had on English.

questions.prompt: According to the speaker, what happened when Middle English emerged?

choices.html: English became the preferred language of authors like Chaucer.
It replaced Old English practically overnight.
English became more subtle and expressive.
English vocabulary exploded.

Match the following historical events with the influence they had on the English language.

Norman Conquest >

Hundred Years' War >

Black Death >

Expansion of Trade and Colonialism >

options: Building a strong English national identity

Increased borrowing of words from other languages

Increased borrowing of words from other languages

questions.prompt: It may be inferred that the Statute of Pleading enacted in 1362 was significant for the English language. Why?

choices.html: It stopped French words from being added to English.
It limited the use of Norman French to legal matters.
It promoted the use of Latin in the administration.
It officially recognized English for use in the administration.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the lecture on desertification?

choices.html: The economic impacts of desertification on global markets.
The causes and direct and indirect effects of desertification.
The role of agriculture in accelerating desertification.
The history and future of desertification in arid regions.

questions.prompt: What is the lecturer's attitude towards the role of human activity in desertification?

choices.html: He believes natural processes are equally to blame.
He thinks human activities are major contributors.
He hopes human activities can solve desertification.
He sees desertification as an inevitable phenomenon.

questions.prompt:
Match the following Contributing Factors to their Effects:

Intensive grazing >

Loss of vegetation >

Deforestation >

Unsustainable agricultural practices >
It may be inferred that habitat fragmentation leads to

choices.html: the endangerment of species.
changes in migrant behavior.
changes in breeding habits.
increased desertification.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker mention Darfur?

choices.html: To illustrate the result of falling crop yields.
To compare the US with a less fortunate country.
To emphasize how serious desertification can be.
To show the vulnerability of subsistence farming.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker mean when he says this?

choices.html: people in the US aren't affected by desertification.
nobody ever thinks they'll be affected by war.
Americans don't appreciate the impact of climate change.
US agricultural practices are much better than elsewhere.
